title: {{NAME}} and the Cretaceous Emergency Squad
moral: The most effective team is one that uses every member's unique abilities.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a dark green hero suit with amber markings, a short cape, and sturdy amber boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The Crisis Response Guild had a problem.

They had received a distress signal from a temporal anomaly: a nest of Pterosaur eggs had been displaced into the present day and were about to hatch in an industrial zone with no appropriate food or habitat.

The Guild's heroes were all in action elsewhere. Available assets: one junior hero ({{NAME}}), one rescue dog (Max), and three experienced woodland animal volunteers from the Park Ranger Program.

"Also," said the radio operator, "a Ankylosaurus has come through the same anomaly and seems stable but confused."

{{NAME}} put on his cape. "On my way."

pages.content:
The eggs were in a loading bay: five of them, leathery and warm, beginning to move.

The Ankylosaurus was in the car park, turning in slow circles and looking increasingly unhappy about concrete.

{{NAME}} divided tasks: Max and the fox tracked the heat signatures of the eggs and confirmed all five were viable. The deer, tall enough to see the area, served as lookout. The badger began excavating a temporary nest area from a patch of earth nearby.

{{NAME}} went to deal with the Ankylosaurus.

pages.content:
The Ankylosaurus needed ground under its feet and something familiar to smell.

The nearby park had both. {{NAME}} led it there with a steady voice and a piece of leafy branch, walking backwards slowly, keeping eye contact.

The Ankylosaurus followed.

In the park, the moment its feet hit grass, it stopped, planted all four feet, and released a breath that sounded like a pressure valve opening.

"Okay," said {{NAME}}. "Stay here. I'll come back."

pages.content:
When he returned to the loading bay, all five eggs had hatched.

Five tiny Pterosaur chicks were being fed a combination of mealworms (from Max's emergency kit), small fish (that the fox had retrieved from a nearby ornamental pond), and something the badger had dug up that {{NAME}} decided not to examine too closely.

The chicks were noisy and demanding and already trying to flap their stub wings.

"How long until the return portal?" {{NAME}} called.

"Thirty minutes," said the radio.

"We have thirty minutes of fish," said the fox, with professional confidence.

pages.content:
All five chicks and the Ankylosaurus went through the return portal with seven minutes to spare.

{{NAME}} stood at the closed portal with his team around him: Max panting happily, the fox cleaning its paw, the badger eating something, the deer looking distinguished.

"Good work," he told them.

The fox looked at him sideways, which he had come to understand meant you too.

In bed that night, he thought about the chick that had grabbed his finger and refused to let go until the portal opened.

He fell asleep smiling, his hand warm where it had held.
